'''''Elaeagnus angustifolia''''', commonly called '''Russian olive''',<ref>{{cite web |title=Russian Olive Species Profile |publisher=USDA |url=https://www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov/profile/russian-olive |access-date=2016-01-10 }}</ref> '''silver berry''',<ref name=HortusIII>{{cite book |author=Bailey, L. H. |author2=Bailey, E. Z. |author3=the staff of the Liberty Hyde Bailey Hortorium |date=1976 |title=Hortus third: A concise dictionary of plants cultivated in the United States and Canada |publisher=Macmillan |location=New York |isbn=978-0-02-505470-7 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/hortusthirdconci00bail }}</ref> '''oleaster''',<ref name=HortusIII /> or '''wild olive''',<ref name=HortusIII /> is a species of ''[[Elaeagnus]]'', native to Asia and limited areas of eastern Europe. It is widely established in North America as an [[introduced species]].<ref name="Sullivan2020">{{cite web | url= http://www.wildflowersearch.com/search?&PlantName=Elaeagnus+angustifolia | last= Sullivan | first= Steven. K. | date= 2020 | title= ''Elaeagnus angustifolia'' | website= Wildflower Search | access-date= 2020-09-22 }}</ref><ref name="PLANTS">{{cite web | url= https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=ELAN | date= 2020 | title= ''Elaeagnus angustifolia'' | author=USDA, NRCS. | website= The PLANTS Database | publisher= National Plant Data Team, Greensboro, NC 27401-4901 USA. | access-date= 2020-09-22}}</ref>

== Description ==
''Elaeagnus angustifolia'' is a thorny [[tree]] growing to {{convert|35|ft|m|abbr=off|order=flip}} in height.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://plants.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=ELAN | title=USDA Plants Database }}</ref> Its stems, buds, and leaves have a dense covering of silvery to rusty scales. The [[leaves]] are alternate, [[lanceolate]], {{convert|4|–|9|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=off}} long and {{convert|1|-|2.5|cm|in|frac=8|abbr=on}} broad, with a smooth margin. The plants begin to flower and fruit from 3 years old. The highly aromatic [[flower]]s, produced in clusters of one to three, are 1 cm long with a four-lobed creamy yellow calyx; they appear in early summer and are followed by clusters of [[fruit]], a small cherry-like [[drupe]] {{convert|1|-|1.7|cm|in|frac=8|abbr=on}} long, orange-red covered in silvery scales. The fruits are about 1 cm wide<ref name="arno2">{{Cite book |last1=Arno |first1=Stephen F. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qDD4DwAAQBAJ |title=Northwest Trees: Identifying & Understanding the Region's Native Trees |last2=Hammerly |first2=Ramona P. |publisher=[[Mountaineers Books]] |year=2020 |isbn=978-1-68051-329-5 |edition=field guide |location=Seattle |pages=287–288 |language=en |oclc=1141235469 |orig-date=1977}}</ref> and sweet, though with a dryish, mealy texture.<ref name="Klinkenberg2020">{{cite web | url= http://linnet.geog.ubc.ca/Atlas/Atlas.aspx?sciname=Elaeagnus%20angustifolia | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20220928181736/http://linnet.geog.ubc.ca/Atlas/Atlas.aspx?sciname=Elaeagnus%20angustifolia | url-status= dead | archive-date= September 28, 2022 | editor-last= Klinkenberg | editor-first= Brian | date= 2020 | title= ''Elaeagnus angustifolia'' | website= E-Flora BC: Electronic Atlas of the Plants of British Columbia [eflora.bc.ca]. | publisher= Lab for Advanced Spatial Analysis, Department of Geography, University of British Columbia, Vancouver | access-date= 2020-09-22 }}</ref><ref name="WTU Herbarium2020">{{cite web | url= http://biology.burke.washington.edu/herbarium/imagecollection/taxon.php?Taxon=Elaeagnus%20angustifolia | editor-last= Giblin | editor-first= David  | date= 2020 | title= ''Elaeagnus angustifolia'' | website= WTU Herbarium Image Collection | publisher= Burke Museum, University of Washington | access-date= 2020-09-22}}</ref><ref name="Jepson">{{cite web | url= http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_IJM.pl?tid=Elaeagnus%20angustifolia | date= 2020 | title= Elaeagnus angustifolia | website= in Jepson Flora Project (eds.) Jepson eFlora | publisher= Jepson Herbarium; University of California, Berkeley | access-date= 2020-09-22}}</ref>

The species is established and reproduced primarily by seed, with some [[vegetative propagation]] also occurring.<ref name="Audubon">{{cite book |last=Little |first=Elbert L. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Western Region |publisher=Knopf |year=1994 |isbn=0-394-50761-4 |edition=Chanticleer Press |page=566 |orig-year=1980}}</ref> The branches have thorns that can be {{convert|2|-|7|cm|in|frac=8|abbr=on}} long.

==Taxonomy and distribution==
The first scientific description of ''Elaeagnus angustifolia'' was by [[Carl Linnaeus]] under its present name in 1753.<ref name="POWO" /> Its common name comes from its similarity in appearance to the [[olive]] (''Olea europaea''), in a different botanical [[Family (taxonomy)|family]], the [[Oleaceae]].

According to Sudnik et al., "Most authors suggest that E. angustifolia originated from the Irano-Turanian region. The species is widely distributed in south-west Asia. In the East its range extends from Kashmir and north-west India to eastern Kazakhstan. The western limit of the species distribution is unclear; the natural character of the tree stands in the lower Volga region (Golub et al. 2002) and Anatolia (Browicz 1996) is questioned."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sudnik-Wójcikowska |first1=Barbara| last2=Moysiyenko |first2=Ivan | last3= Slim |first3=Pieter A.|last4= Moraczewski |first4=Ireneusz R. |title=Impact of the invasive species Elaeagnus Angustifolia L. on vegetation in pontic desert steppe Zone (Southern Ukraine) |journal=Polish Journal of Ecology |date=2009 |volume=57 |issue=2 |pages=269-281 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/280100347_Impact_of_the_invasive_species_Elaeagnus_Angustifolia_L_on_vegetation_in_pontic_desert_steppe_ZONE_Southern_Ukraine |access-date=29 June 2026}}</ref>

Further east in Asia, the native range stretches into Afghanistan, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and the nations of the [[Caucasus]]. In India they are found in the western [[Himalayas]]. There is a [[disjunct population]] in Myanmar and [[Assam]] in eastern India. They grow natively in Mongolia and in China they are found in the north-central, southeast, [[Inner Mongolia]], [[Manchuria]], [[Qinghai]], and [[Xinjiang]].<ref name="POWO" />

== Ecology ==
[[File:Cienega2.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|Russian olive invading a rare [[ciénega]] in [[New Mexico]], United States]]

The shrub possesses a high level of salinity tolerance [https://plants.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=ELAN]<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/tree/elaang/all.html |title=Forest Service Fire Ecology |access-date=2008-01-15 |archive-date=2008-04-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080405152020/http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/tree/elaang/all.html |url-status=live }}</ref> enabling it to grow on bare mineral substrates and poor, eroded soils and environments.

The caterpillars of the high altitude alpine moth ''[[Lachana alpherakii]]'' use it as a [[host plant]].<ref name="Trofimova2008">{{cite journal |last=Trofimova |first=Tatyana A. |date=January 2008 |title=Systematic notes on ''Dasorgyia'' Staudinger, 1881, ''Dicallomera'' Butler, 1881, and ''Lachana'' Moore, 1888 (Lymantriidae) |url=http://www.soceurlep.eu/uploads/nota/bd31_2/09_Trofimova.pdf |journal=Nota Lepidopterologica |volume=31 |issue=2 |pages=273–291 |issn=0342-7536 |access-date=26 November 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120423063917/http://www.soceurlep.eu/tl_files/nota/bd31_2/09_Trofimova.pdf |archive-date=23 April 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The fruit is readily eaten and the seeds disseminated by many species of birds.

=== Invasive behavior ===
The species was introduced into North America by the late 19th century, and was both planted and spread through the consumption of its fruits (which seldom ripen in [[England]]),<ref>Parkinson noted that it rarely perfected its fruit (noted by Coats 1992).</ref> by birds, which disperse the [[seeds]].<ref name="Audubon" /> Russian olive is considered to be an [[invasive species]] in many places in the [[United States]] because it thrives on poor soil, has high seedling survival rates, matures in a few years, and out-competes the native vegetation. It often invades riparian habitats where the canopy of [[Populus sect. Aegiros|cottonwood]] trees has died. Its quick-spreading root system can make it [[pest (organism)|pest]]-like.

== Uses ==
[[File:Haft Mewa Afghan Dish.jpg|alt=A colorful bowl of mixed dried fruits viewed from above, sitting on a flowered cloth|thumb|Dried oleaster fruit (''senjed'') among other fruits as part of ''haft mēwa'', an Afghan dish]]

It is widely grown across southern and central Europe as a drought- and cold-resistant [[ornamental plant]] for its scented flowers, edible fruit,<ref name="arno2" /> attractive yellow foliage and black bark.<ref name="Audubon" /> It was grown in England by [[John Parkinson (botanist)|John Parkinson]] no later than 1633.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Coats |first1=Alice M. |last2=Creech |first2=John L. |title=Garden Shrubs and Their Histories |date=1992 |publisher=Simon and Schuster |location=New York |isbn=978-0-671-74733-6 |page=75 |edition=1st US |url=https://archive.org/details/gardenshrubsthei0000coat/page/75 |access-date=2 May 2024 |language=en}}</ref>

In Iran, the dried powder of the fruit is used mixed with milk for rheumatoid arthritis and joint pains. There is evidence supporting beneficial effects of aqueous extract of Persian olive in reducing the symptoms of [[osteoarthritis]] with an efficacy comparable to that of [[acetaminophen]] and [[ibuprofen]].<ref>{{Cite journal |pmc = 4908661|year = 2016|last1 = Panahi|first1 = Y.|title = Efficacy of Elaeagnus Angustifolia extract in the treatment of knee osteoarthritis: A randomized controlled trial|journal = Excli Journal|volume = 15|pages = 203–210|last2 = Alishiri|first2 = G. H.|last3 = Bayat|first3 = N.|last4 = Hosseini|first4 = S. M.|last5 = Sahebkar|first5 = A.|pmid = 27330526|doi = 10.17179/excli2015-639}}</ref>

It is one of the seven items used in [[Haft-sin]], a traditional table setting of [[Nowruz]], the traditional Persian spring celebration. The [[dried fruit]], known locally as ''senjed'', is one of seven served in its own [[syrup]] in a [[fruit salad]] called ''haft mēwa'' eaten during [[Nowruz in Afghanistan]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Sethi |first=Simran |date=2022-03-21 |title=Nowruz is banned in Afghanistan, but families continue to celebrate |language=en |work=NPR |url=https://www.npr.org/2022/03/21/1087296594/nowruz-is-banned-in-afghanistan-but-families-continue-to-celebrate |access-date=2022-04-29}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Deravian |first=Naz |date=2022-03-14 |title=For Afghans Abroad, Nowruz Is a Chance to Reflect |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/03/14/dining/afghan-nowroz-celebration-food.html |access-date=2022-04-29 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

In folk herbalism Russian olive has a wide variety of uses. The leaves, fruit, flowers, and bark are all employed. The leaves are known to help in the gastrointestinal system, assist in wound healing and are used as an antibacterial. The fruit has a wide range of traditional applications, including use as an anti-inflammatory and antioxidant. The flowers are a traditional remedy for fevers, made as an herbal infusion.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Farzaei |first1=Mohammad Hosein |last2=Bahramsoltani |first2=Roodabeh |last3=Abbasabadi |first3=Zahra |last4=Rahimi |first4=Roja |date=2015-11-01 |title=A comprehensive review on phytochemical and pharmacological aspects of ''Elaeagnus angustifolia'' L. |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/jphp.12442 |journal=Journal of Pharmacy and Pharmacology |volume=67 |issue=11 |pages=1467–1480 |doi=10.1111/jphp.12442 |pmid=26076872 |issn=2042-7158}}</ref>

In urban settings, landscapers use plantings of Russian olive to discourage people from resting or sleeping in the location.<ref>Fenton, Mike. [https://www.asisonline.org/security-management-magazine/articles/2008/05/discouraging-loiterers-by-design/ Discouraging Loiterers by Design] Security Management, 01 May 2008.</ref>

== Chemistry ==
''E. angustifolia'' contains the alkaloids [[harmine]], [[harmane]], and [[harmol]] in the roots and shoot, as well as [[calligonine]] in the bark.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Elaeagnus angustifolia {{!}} Plant {{!}} Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases |url=https://phytochem.nal.usda.gov/plant-elaeagnus-angustifolia |access-date=2024-01-21 |website=phytochem.nal.usda.gov}}</ref>
